title: The First 7 Days — An Inheritance Walkthrough
rule_one: Nothing is urgent. While the words are only in your hands, Bitcoin cannot be stolen by waiting. It can be lost by rushing. Every irreversible mistake in Bitcoin happens in minutes; every safe step can be taken calmly. You have time. Use it. One exception: if the words may already have left his control — a photo, a cloud backup, an email draft, anything typed into a phone or website — closing that leak is the one urgent thing. You close it by securing the exposed copy, or by securing and then moving the funds — never by rushing the wallet work itself.

days.title: Secure the paper, touch nothing
days.goal: lose nothing. Recover nothing. Change nothing
dos: Collect everything Bitcoin-related into one box you control: - Any hardware wallets, USB sticks, cards with a chip (Ledger, BitBox02, Jade, Trezor, Coldcard, Bitkey) - Any papers with handwritten or printed lists of words (12 or 24, or numbered groups — sometimes split across pages) - Any "wallet files", USB drives labeled with wallet names, letters of instruction, envelopes with instructions - Anything metal with words/letters stamped or punched into it
Keep the box somewhere safe and normal (a lockable drawer, a safe).
Write down (on paper, not in the app) *where you found each thing*.
donts: Do not plug anything in yet.
Do not reset, format, "clean up", or wipe any device — even if it seems locked or broken.
Do not photograph word lists. Phones automatically back up photos to the cloud, and a photo of a seed phrase is a permanent leak.
Do not type the words into any app, website, or this app.
Do not delete anything on his computer or phone — "wallet" files, "Ledger Live", "Sparrow", "Electrum" — nothing.
Do not tell anyone what you found or how much there is.

days.title: Make a written inventory (no secrets on the page)
days.goal: know what you have, in plain words, on your own paper
dos: What it physically is ("small black device, buttons, 'Ledger' on back")
Where it was found ("second drawer of his desk")
Anything written on it or its packaging ("label says 'main'")
Safe deposit box? Home safe? Attorney's office? Bank vault?
A laptop he used alone (check browser bookmarks later — Day 4)
An app on his phone: "Sparrow", "BlueWallet", "Muun", "Nunchuk", "River", "Strike", "Cash App", "Coinbase" — list the names, open nothing yet.
donts: Never write the seed words themselves into the inventory. The inventory page is a plain paper list — write only "24-word list found, sealed envelope, 3 pages." A written copy of the words is a second copy that can be lost, seen, or stolen.

days.title: Learn what each thing is (the app explains, the box stays closed)
dos: "What is a seed phrase?" (5 min)
"What is a hardware wallet?" (5 min)
"What is Sparrow / Ledger Live / an exchange account?" (5 min each)
"What is multisig? What is a 'descriptor' file?" (10 min — only if you found 2+ hardware wallets or a file mentioning '2 of 3')

days.title: Look, don't touch (verification with open eyes)
days.goal: understand the setup's shape without entering any secrets anywhere
dos: Word lists: confirm each list is complete (the number of words it claims — usually 24). Look for extra instructions on the paper ("add this word when restoring" = a passphrase; note that it exists, do not combine it with anything yet).

Devices: note their brand and model from the packaging or the back of the device. Do not power them on yet. (Some devices erase after wrong PIN attempts — you will power them on only when you have both the PIN *and* the backup words, later.)
His computer: open his browser bookmarks. Wallet-related bookmarks are safe to *look at* (websites like sparrowwallet.com, ledger.com). Do not log into anything; just note the names.

Exchange accounts (River, Strike, Swan, Coinbase…): you can see whether an account exists without touching funds. Do not try to reset passwords today — account recovery is a legal/identity process you will do deliberately in Day 5–6 with documents in hand.
donts: Do not power any device on yet. Some devices erase themselves after too many wrong PIN attempts — you will power them on only when you have both the PIN *and* the backup words, later.
Do not log into anything. Look at bookmarks and account names only; today is look, not touch.
Do not try to reset any account password today. Account recovery is a legal/identity process you will do deliberately in Day 5–6 with documents in hand.

days.title: Know your options (no action yet)
days.goal: understand the three honest paths forward
dos: Read the three paths and open the app's deep-dive guide for the one you want to understand first.
Settle for today on learning, not choosing — the only decision today is *which guide to read first*.
donts: Don't move any bitcoin to a custodian today. Path B means the keys were used, and it is only ever done after you have practiced recovering the wallet yourself — never because a stranger suggested it.
Don't hire anyone who calls themselves a "recovery expert." Complex estates call for a Bitcoin-knowledgeable estate attorney; the app never picks a paid professional for you.

days.title: Assemble your verification plan
days.goal: a written plan for the first real action, which is always the same: prove you can open the wallet without risking anything
dos: A clean computer — a separate one. A new machine, or your own computer used offline. Never his. "Clean" means a dedicated offline machine, or a freshly installed operating system you control. The app's guide explains what "clean" means and why. Seed words are never entered on a networked or possibly-compromised machine.
The wallet software — downloaded only from the official site, with the checksum verification the guide walks you through (this is where the app earns its keep — verification is mechanical and safe).

The order of operations — the non-negotiable sequence: 1. Install the software. 2. Verify the download. 3. Restore the wallet. - Hardware wallet first, if there is one. Enter its PIN on the device — never on a computer. If the wallet must be restored, the device asks for the words itself, and they are entered on the device too. (Some devices erase themselves after too many wrong PIN attempts — which is why the backup words are confirmed before any power-on.) - No hardware wallet? Then the words are typed ONCE, into the verified recovery software on the clean machine. This is the single exception to Day 1's "do not type the words into any app, website, or this app." The only place the words may ever be typed: wallet-recovery software that was checksum-verified, running on a clean machine. Nowhere else. 4. Write down the first receiving address. 5. Confirm the balance appears (or ask the app why it doesn't). 6. Nothing else. No sending, no "upgrading", no swapping wallets the same day.
A helper rule: one difficult thing per day. Two in one day is how mistakes happen.
donts: Never wipe, reset, or reinstall his computer — not today, not while the estate is unsettled. It may hold wallet files, descriptor files, and browser bookmarks that count as evidence. Wiping it destroys them. His old laptop is *not* your clean machine. Day 1's rule stands until the estate is settled.

days.title: Rest, then repeat what worked
dos: Re-read your inventory and your Day 6 plan.

Do nothing irreversible. If you completed Day 6's verification and saw the balance, you have already done the hardest part — and it was done *without spending anything, without sharing anything, and without trusting anyone.*
Start the next phase at your pace: the app's guides on "spending safely", "moving to your own custody", "tax basics", and the directory are there when you're ready.
